excerpt: The Voladores of Tamaletón are a living Teenek ritual near Tancanhuitz. When to go, what it costs, and how to drive there from Ciudad Valles.
contentHtml:
The Voladores of Tamaletón (the "flyers") are a sacred Teenek ritual performed at the Tamaletón Ceremonial Center, in the municipality of Tancanhuitz de Santos, San Luis Potosí. The Voladores of Tamaletón are one of the most living expressions of the Indigenous worldview of the Huasteca Potosina: four dancers spin down from the top of a pole more than twenty meters tall while a fifth musician plays flute and drum at the very top. If you want to witness this rite without finding the site closed or showing up out of season, this guide solves exactly that.

In this guide you'll find schedules, the admission price, the exact route from Ciudad Valles, and the months with the most activity for the Huasteca voladores dance. High season for the ritual in Tamaletón, Tancanhuitz runs from December to February.

At www.huasteca-potosina.com we work with local guides and operators across the region. This guide is updated with real experiences from people who travel the Huasteca Potosina every week. Last updated: October 2026. If you'd rather arrive with everything arranged, check out our all-inclusive packages to see the Voladores of Tamaletón.

The Teenek ritual of the Voladores of Tamaletón: origin and meaning

What exactly is the Teenek voladores ritual?

The Teenek ritual of the voladores is a ceremony of fertility and communication with the sky deities. Four men, the voladores, climb a ritual pole called the palo volador and launch themselves off tied by the feet, spinning as they descend for exactly 13 turns each. That adds up to 52 rotations in total, the same number as the cycle of the Mesoamerican calendar. At Tamaletón, unlike more folklorized versions, the ceremony keeps Teenek linguistic and choreographic elements you won't find at other centers in the country. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) declared the voladores dance an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009, and the Tamaletón community is one of the few groups that has kept the rite going from generation to generation with no documented interruptions.

The groups we host from Ciudad Valles often ask whether the ceremony is a show for tourists. The honest answer is that at Tamaletón the ritual follows its own ceremonial calendar, with dates tied to the farming cycle and to patron saint festivals. The busiest days, Thursday through Sunday, line up with the days it's open to the public, but the dance isn't performed only for visitors: there are internal ceremonies that happen even when no one is in the viewing area. That's what makes the difference. Book the Surrealist Route if you want to add the Castillo de la Salud, Las Pozas, and the Huichihuayán Spring on another day of your trip.

Where is the Tamaletón Ceremonial Center?

The Ceremonial Center is in the community of Tamaletón, in the municipality of Tancanhuitz de Santos, about 3.6 km from downtown Tancanhuitz along the road toward San Antonio. The final stretch to the grounds is a 1 km track from the property entrance, passable in a regular car during the dry season and best done only in a high-clearance truck during heavy rain. The site has a parking area, basic restrooms, and vendors selling Teenek crafts on weekends.

For more background on the Indigenous culture of this part of the Huasteca Potosina, see our guide to the traditions and music of Huastec culture, where we explain the role of the Teenek people in the region.

When can you see the Voladores of Tamaletón? 2026 season and schedule

High season: December to February, the ideal time

The main season to see the Voladores of Tamaletón runs from December to February. During these months the ceremonial cycle picks up because it coincides with the Teenek year-end festivities and with the dry season, which makes it easier to reach the Ceremonial Center. According to local guides who work in Tamaletón, Tancanhuitz, the days with the most flights are Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday; Monday through Wednesday there's still some activity, but noticeably less, and it may be limited to rehearsals or internal preparations. The best time to arrive is between 10:00 AM and 1:00 PM, when the light is good for photos and the heat isn't overwhelming yet.

The travelers we coordinate in the Huasteca Potosina often pair Tamaletón with Aquismón on the same day. The distance between the two is manageable, so you can see the Huasteca voladores dance in the morning and explore the archaeological site or the lookouts of Aquismón in the afternoon. See our guide to Aquismón, Pueblo Mágico: what to see and how to get there to plan that combination. See available tours in the Huasteca Potosina.

Admission price and costs at the Ceremonial Center

Admission to the Tamaletón Ceremonial Center costs $100 MXN per person (about US$6 at the 2026 exchange rate). The fee goes straight to the community and pays for upkeep of the palo volador and the ceremonial materials. In practice there's no separate rate by age, though it's a good idea to ask at the ticket booth if you're traveling with small children. Operators in Tancanhuitz offer trips from Ciudad Valles that include transportation, a guide, and admission; prices vary by group and season, so it's best to ask directly in the municipality or through verified agencies.

If you're planning a bigger trip around the region, our guide on how much it costs to visit the Huasteca Potosina will help you put together a realistic budget with up-to-date numbers. For options with lodging included, check out our all-inclusive packages.

Tips before you visit the Voladores of Tamaletón

Showing up well prepared makes the difference between a smooth visit and a frustrating afternoon. Access is easy in the dry season, but a few logistical details can complicate the trip if you don't plan for them. Keep the following in mind before you head out.

  • Confirm the active days before you go: even though the main season runs from December to February, activity is minimal Monday through Wednesday. Showing up on a Tuesday that isn't a holiday may mean finding the site with no flights scheduled.
  • Bring cash in Mexican pesos: the Ceremonial Center's ticket booth doesn't take cards. Bring at least $200 MXN per person for admission, a tip, and a local craft if something catches your eye.
  • Closed-toe shoes and light clothing: the last kilometer of the access road is packed dirt with loose stones. Flat sandals or flip-flops are uncomfortable; sneakers or closed shoes make the walk much easier. The weather in Tancanhuitz during high season is warm and dry, with temperatures between 22 and 32 °C.
  • Don't interrupt the ritual with your flash: the community allows photos and video, but a direct flash while the dancers climb and descend the pole can distract them. Use silent mode and natural light; your photos will turn out better, too.
  • Pair it with Xantolo if you're traveling in October: even though it doesn't line up with the main season, visiting the region in October lets you add the Huastec Day of the Dead festival to your itinerary. See our guide to Xantolo in the Huasteca Potosina to understand the full cultural calendar.
  • Check the dirt road during the rainy season: from June to September, the rain can make the road to the grounds impassable for two-wheel-drive vehicles. If you're traveling in those months, check road conditions with local operators before leaving Ciudad Valles. Our guide to Huasteca Potosina weather in October explains how rain affects access roads in the region.

How do you get to the Voladores of Tamaletón from Ciudad Valles?

Ciudad Valles is the most common starting point for visiting Tamaletón, Tancanhuitz. The route is direct, mostly well signposted, and you don't need a guide to drive it on your own. The groups we host every season do it without trouble in standard vehicles during the dry months.

Driving route from Ciudad Valles: step by step

From Ciudad Valles, take the México–Laredo highway toward Tamazunchale. Drive 52 km to the Xolol–Tamuín junction, which is about 60 minutes of driving at normal speed. At that junction, turn left toward Tancanhuitz; in about 7 minutes you'll reach the town center. From there, turn left toward the community of San Antonio and go 3.6 km (about 10 minutes more). The sign for the Ceremonial Center appears before you reach San Antonio; from that point there's a final 1 km of dirt road to the parking lot. All in all, the full drive from Ciudad Valles takes 75 to 90 minutes without stops.

Transportation options and costs compared

If you're not driving your own car, there are transportation options from Tancanhuitz, although none goes directly to the Ceremonial Center. Mototaxis from downtown Tancanhuitz to the start of the dirt road charge between $40 and $60 MXN per person. From there you'll have to walk or hire someone to take you the last kilometer. The most comfortable option if you don't have a vehicle is a local operator with transportation included, available through agencies in the municipality. Also see our guide to the best time to visit the Huasteca Potosina and plan the rest of your itinerary from there. Frequently asked questions about the Voladores of Tamaletón

Do the Voladores of Tamaletón perform every day of the year?

No. The main season is December to February. During that time the site is busiest Thursday through Sunday; Monday through Wednesday there are fewer performances. Outside the season, the Ceremonial Center may take visitors with fewer flights, or only on special feast days of the Teenek calendar.

How much does it cost to enter the Tamaletón Ceremonial Center?

Admission is $100 MXN per person (about US$6 in 2026). You pay in cash at the ticket booth. There's no ATM at the entrance, so bring cash from Ciudad Valles or Tancanhuitz.

How long does it take to get there from Ciudad Valles, and what's the best season?

The drive from Ciudad Valles takes 75 to 90 minutes: 52 km on the México–Laredo highway to the Tancanhuitz junction, plus 3.6 km toward San Antonio and a final 1 km of dirt road to the grounds. The best season is December to February, when there are more performances and access is safer thanks to the dry season.

Is it a good idea to bring kids or older adults to see the Huasteca voladores dance at Tamaletón?

Yes, the Teenek ritual of the Voladores of Tamaletón is suitable for all ages. The grounds have a ground-level viewing area, and there's no long walking involved. For older adults with limited mobility, the only obstacle is the kilometer of dirt road at the entrance; in the dry season you can drive it all the way to the parking lot near the flight area.

Saturdays between 10:00 AM and 1:00 PM are the busiest hours to witness the Teenek ritual at the Tamaletón Ceremonial Center.
